domain: Religious Studies / Japanese History / Ontology of Practice
topic_summary: Analysis of shinbutsu-shugo (Shinto-Buddhist syncretism) in pre-Meiji Japan, examining whether centuries of simultaneous practice constituted a single fused ontological commitment or a domain-partitioned coexistence. The kernel contest centers on whether the syncretic reading (one unified cosmology) and the partition reading (separate jurisdictions for life-cycle vs afterlife) represent coherent interpretations of the same commitment or expose an incoherent bundle that only appeared stable due to institutional tolerance.

key_entities: Kami (Shinto deities, nature spirits, ancestral presences)
Honji-suijaku theory (doctrinal framework: kami as local manifestations of universal buddhas)
Meiji government (1868+ state apparatus enforcing shinbutsu-bunri separation)
Village practitioners (lay population maintaining dual ritual participation)
key_tensions: Ontological unity vs jurisdictional partition (syncretic vs domain-partition readings)
Institutional fusion vs doctrinal incoherence (jingu-ji practice vs philosophical consistency)
key_claims: Honji-suijaku provided a coherent metaphysical framework unifying kami and buddhas under one cosmology
Practitioners treated Shinto and Buddhism as separate domains (birth/marriage vs death/afterlife) without ontological integration
The Meiji shinbutsu-bunri separation was violently disruptive, indicating prior fusion was structurally deep
The ease of institutional separation in some regions suggests the fusion was shallow, a modus vivendi rather than ontological commitment
key_mechanisms: Honji-suijaku doctrine (buddhas as 'original ground,' kami as 'trace manifestations')
Ritual domain allocation (Shinto for purification/fertility, Buddhism for funerary/soteriological)
Meiji shinbutsu-bunri enforcement (legal separation, destruction of jingu-ji, forced clergy reclassification)
key_absences: Practitioner testimony on ontological coherence (historical record dominated by elite doctrinal texts)
Regional variation in fusion depth (urban temple-shrine vs rural village practice)

omegas.description: Historical record lacks direct practitioner testimony on ontological coherence. Elite doctrinal texts may not reflect village-level cosmology. Syncretic reading may be a Buddhist institutional projection onto non-doctrinal practice.

Urban temple-shrine complexes vs rural village practice may have exhibited different fusion depths. Meiji separation ease varied regionally, suggesting heterogeneous kernel stability. Partition reading may be regionally valid while syncretic reading holds in institutional centers.

Honji-suijaku doctrine privileges Buddhist ontology (buddhas as 'original,' kami as 'traces'). This asymmetry may indicate syncretic reading was a Buddhist absorption strategy rather than genuine fusion. If so, partition reading better describes practitioner autonomy.

Would shinbutsu-shugo have persisted without Meiji intervention? Incoherence reading depends on separation ease as evidence, but state violence may have disrupted a stable equilibrium. Absence of separation attempt in Tokugawa period is weak evidence for stability.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The ontological status of kami and buddhas in pre-Meiji Japan — whether they constituted one fused cosmological order, separate jurisdictional domains, or an incoherent bundle tolerated by institutional flexibility
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Doctrinal authority resided in Buddhist scholastic tradition (honji-suijaku texts) and Shinto priestly lineages, but practitioner autonomy in ritual allocation suggests weak interpretive monopoly. Meiji state imposed external authority via legal separation.

axiom_contradictions.basis: Syncretic reading requires ontological unity (kami ARE buddha-manifestations); partition reading requires ontological separation (kami and buddhas are distinct entities in separate domains). No single framework holds both: either they are one thing or two things.
Syncretic reading asserts a coherent unified cosmology; incoherence reading asserts no coherent cosmology existed. These are contradictory meta-claims about whether a stable kernel was present.
Partition reading asserts a stable domain-separation framework; incoherence reading asserts no stable framework existed. Partition is a coherence claim; incoherence denies all coherence claims.
